transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-21 | Time: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 52m
Recording id: FF-20260621-4829
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Halcyon - Lead ML), Sofia Martinez (Halcyon - Frontend), Liam O'Neil (Halcyon - CTO)

Summary (auto): Quick onramp showing hosted API streaming, parameter guidance, and failure handling patterns. Emphasis on how to keep tail latency low while controlling cost.

[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex Martinez, I'll run the quick onramp and Priya will jump into the demo. Quick confirm — Jordan, Liam, Sofia — can you hear us all okay?
[00:06] Jordan (Lead ML): Yeah, good loud and clear.
[00:08] Sofia (Frontend): Yep, good.
[00:10] Liam (CTO): All set.
[00:12] Alex: Cool. Goal for today: show Redwood's hosted chat/text generation basics — streaming, common params, and our retry/fallback patterns. We’ll also touch on cost/latency tradeoffs for your expected workload. Sound good?
[00:22] Liam: Sounds right. We mostly want to understand tail latency behavior and how retries affect cost. Also curious on SSO and KMS for logs.
[00:28] Alex: Great. Priya?
[00:30] Priya (SE): Thanks. I'll share my screen. First slide is a very short architecture: client -> Redwood hosted API -> model runtime. We'll demo the streaming endpoint which returns token deltas as they generate, so you can render in the UI as text appears.
[00:45] Priya: One quick note, streaming is "chunked" — sometimes you'll see partial tokens or broken words mid-stream if tokenization splits in the middle, so the client should be able to append fragments. We also recommend a short debounce in the UI to avoid janky rerenders.
[01:05] Jordan: How big are the chunks typically? Is it per token or per 64 token window?
[01:10] Priya: Good q. It depends on model and runtime; usually you get token-level deltas but network batching or internal flushes can cluster a few tokens together. In our logs you'll see both single-token events and bursts of 4-10 tokens.
[01:23] Jordan: OK. On the topic of retries, if a streaming connection drops mid-response, what's the recourse? Do we have to re-issue the entire prompt?
[01:30] Priya: We have a couple of patterns. For idempotent requests — like stateless completion — you can retry with idempotency keys; Redwood supports request ids so the backend can resume or dedupe. For chat stateful flows we recommend checkpointing the last confirmed assistant message client-side and re-requesting from that point. There's also a recommended backoff policy: exponential with jitter, and a hard cap after 3 attempts for typical hosted usage.
[01:56] Sofia: Does resuming require a special stream token or is it purely via request metadata?
[02:01] Priya: It's via request metadata and the session state you pass. We also have optional KV/prefix caching for common prefixes (e.g., system+history) so repeated requests skip compute for earlier tokens and only generate tail — that helps when re-issuing.
[02:17] Liam: The KV cache sounds promising — is that available for hosted or only Dedicated?
[02:21] Alex: Hosted supports prefix caching for eligible models; Dedicated gives more control over cache sizing and retention policies. We'll send the exact model list that supports caching.
[02:31] Jordan: Cool. Could you show the live streaming demo and then we can throw some failure modes at it?
[02:36] Priya: Yep I'll demo a simple chat completion using the /v1/generate-stream endpoint.
[02:44] [Screen share - terminal]
[02:46] Priya: Here is a curl sample and a small Node snippet. I'll fire a prompt that requests a product blurb from a retail catalog.
[02:55] Priya (typing): "Write a 40 word blurb for product X — highlight eco materials and fast shipping."
[03:05] [03:05] Priya: You can see the stream returning partials: 'Write a 40...' then 'word blurb...' and so on. The client appended fragments smoothly.
[03:20] Jordan: That looks pretty snappy. What's the latency for first token on average?
[03:25] Priya: For these models we typically see first token latency ~80-120ms in us-west, but it varies with context length — longer histories push that up. We can show more detailed percentiles in Console later.
[03:38] Sofia: If we have a web UI with 200ms render target, do you recommend prefetching or streaming real-time?
[03:44] Priya: Streaming is best for perceived responsiveness. Prefetching can help for short templated replies; another option is to send a short stub reply quickly then expand. Depends on UX.
[03:53] Alex: Jordan, earlier you mentioned 100k msgs/day. Do you have a token estimate per message?
[03:59] Jordan: Rough avg 250 tokens in and 60 out. Mostly multi-turn.
[04:05] Alex: Good to know. We'll include cost estimates in the follow-up.
[04:09] [04:09] Priya: Now I'll simulate a mid-stream disconnect and show the retry strategy.
[04:14] Priya (typing): I'm dropping the TCP socket from my side to emulate network blip.
[04:18] [04:18] Priya: You can see the stream truncated with an error event. Client retries with idempotency key and the runtime uses prefix cache to only regenerate tail tokens — the response resumes from token boundary and client re-concatenates.
[04:35] Jordan: In that resumed case — does that double-charge us for the tokens regenerated?
[04:39] Priya: Because of caching and partial resume, you generally only pay for the new compute; however if we can't dedupe (e.g., no cache hit) you may pay for regenerate. For hosted, we optimize for implicit dedupe where possible. We'll include exact cost model notes.
[04:56] Liam: For compliance we need to ensure logs are encrypted at rest and can be sent to our SIEM. What are the logging and KMS options?
[05:04] Alex: Hosted supports envelope encryption and integrates with several KMS providers; for audit logs we have streaming audit event exports and can push to customer-owned Cloud Storage or SIEM via connector. We'll attach SOC 2 and our security whitepaper.
[05:20] Sofia: How does data residency work? We have EU customers and need EU-only processing for PII.
[05:25] Priya: You can pin requests to region endpoints and we support EU-only processing and retention controls on hosted accounts. For strict residency or air-gapped needs, Private or Dedicated on-prem is available.
[05:36] Jordan: Regarding parameters — temperature, top_p, max_tokens — can you show a quick live comparison of outputs?
[05:42] Priya: Sure. I'll run the same prompt with temp=0.0, 0.7 and 1.0 and capture first 3 responses.
[05:50] [06:00] Priya: Temp 0.0 yields deterministic, concise phrasing. Temp 0.7 adds variability and creative phrasing. Temp 1.0 increases diversity but can be less stable. For safety and UI consistency we often recommend 0.2–0.6 for product copy.
[06:20] Jordan: Do you have per-request token limits? We have some long contexts from user profiles that could hit 8k tokens.
[06:26] Alex: We support multiple model sizes; max context depends on model. For long contexts we recommend prefix caching and truncation strategies. If you need >8k context, we can recommend models and hosting patterns or Dedicated where we can select models with extended context.
[06:41] Liam: On cost controls, can we set per-route quotas and alerting?
[06:45] Alex: Yes, Console supports per-route quotas, token spend alerts, and token-level cost breakdowns. You can also rate limit from client-side and set hard caps on API keys.
[06:58] Jordan: Let's talk about burst behavior. We'll have spiky traffic at 10am PST — can hosted handle it or do we need Dedicated?
[07:06] Priya: Hosted has autoscaling and burst tiers; for predictable, sustained high throughput Dedicated is recommended. Hosted is fine for spiky traffic up to a certain egress; we can provide the target QPS numbers based on your peak.
[07:20] Jordan: Anything around idempotency and dedupe for multi-request conversational flows we should be aware of?
[07:25] Priya: Keep client-generated ids for each user-turn and use them on retries. For streaming we also encourage clients to save the last confirmed assistant token offset.
[07:36] Sofia: A practical question: when a stream sends partial tokens you mentioned debouncing in the UI — what duration is safe? 50ms? 150ms?
[07:44] Priya: 100–200ms debounce usually feels right; shorter if you want very low latency but tolerate more reflows.
[07:52] [08:00] Alex: Let's walk through a failure playbook: network blip, runtime OOM, and model fallback. Priya, can you trigger a runtime simulated OOM on a low-memory model?
[08:09] Priya: Sure — switching to a heavy prompt and forcing a low-memory config.
[08:16] [08:16] Priya: Server returned an internal error. Our runtime automatically reroutes to a compatible model variant if configured for fallback. You can set policy in Console: fallback to smaller model, to different region, or to a cached/partial response.
[08:35] Jordan: If fallback to smaller model occurs—how do we know quality degraded? Is there a header or flag?
[08:40] Priya: Good point. We attach metered response metadata in headers and Console events — you get model id, fallback reason, and confidence metrics where available. That way your app can surface an indicator or trigger a re-ask.
[08:55] Liam: For audits, can we get per-request metadata for 30 days? We need traceability.
[09:00] Alex: Hosted retains request logs with metadata for configurable retention; enterprise tiers offer longer retention and export options. We'll share retention matrices.
[09:12] Jordan: Let's push the system: can you run a quick synthetic benchmark — 50 concurrent streams generating 60-token responses — just so we can eyeball latencies?
[09:21] Priya: We can run a mini benchmark; for demo I've got a script. Kicking it now.
[09:30] [09:30] Priya: Running 50 concurrent workers... 
[09:40] [09:40] Priya: Results are shown in the Console: p50 ~120ms, p95 ~420ms, p99 ~920ms for this model under this payload.
[09:52] Jordan: p99 ~920ms is a bit high for us — mostly concerned about tail. Is that mostly network or compute?
[09:59] Priya: Tail often comes from scheduling jitter, cache misses, and context size variance. We can reduce p99 with tighter instance pinning (Dedicated), smarter batching configs, and increasing prefix caching hit rate.
[10:12] Alex: Also, automatic proactive warm pools help for workloads that are very bursty to reduce cold-starts.
[10:19] Sofia: About function calling and structured outputs — does streaming support tool calls or is that synchronous?
[10:25] Priya: Streaming supports tool-calling signals; we stream the assistant tokens up to the function call and then either stream the function args or finish and call out. There are nuances but it's supported. We'll share examples.
[10:40] Jordan: For deployment — we have internal security review. What paperwork do you have?
[10:44] Alex: We have SOC 2 Type II, ISO certs, a data processing addendum (DPA), and an architecture security whitepaper. We'll attach them.
[10:54] Liam: Is SSO available for Console?
[10:56] Priya: Yes, SSO with SAML/SCIM for user provisioning and RBAC is supported on enterprise tiers.
[11:04] Jordan: Any obvious gotchas when moving from dev to prod around tokenization differences or prompt engineering?
[11:10] Priya: Tokenization is deterministic but pretrained tokenizer variants can cause slight token count differences if you swap models. Be mindful when cutting tokens to fit limits; prefer semantic truncation at utterance boundaries.
[11:23] Alex: Before we wrap, any other red flags or must-have items for procurement?
[11:28] Liam: Pricing transparency, SLAs, and a path to Dedicated if usage grows. Also KMS integration and audit export for SOC requirements.
[11:36] Alex: Noted. We'll include Dedicated pricing scenarios and SLA docs.
[11:41] Jordan: One last tech question — does Redwood provide client libs for automatic reconnection and stream reassembly?
[11:46] Priya: Yes, we have SDKs with stream helpers for Node, Python, and a lightweight JS library that handles token reassembly and idempotency helpers. We'll share links.
[11:58] Sofia: Nice.
[12:00] Alex: OK we'll do a quick recap of next steps and action items.
[12:04] Alex: Summary: shared demo of streaming behavior, debounce guidance, retry and idempotency patterns, fallback policies, and security/region options. Follow-ups: quickstart repo, cost estimates, sample prompts, and procurement discussion.
[12:22] Liam: Sounds good. When can we expect the quickstart?
[12:25] Alex: I'll send it tomorrow (2026-06-22) with snippets; Priya will attach a small benchmark config.
[12:31] Jordan: Great. Any blockers on our side? We'll gather prompts and token stats.
[12:35] Alex: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[12:38] [End of meeting - 16:52 UTC approx]
